title: Abdominal pain, diarrhoea and vomiting in a 69-year-old woman
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 69-year-old woman with sudden diffuse crampy abdominal pain, watery diarrhoea and vomiting after contact with a sick grandchild. The candidate then interprets her observations, bloods, venous gas and ECG, recognises acute gastroenteritis with dehydration and a prerenal acute kidney injury, and manages her fluids, her regular medicines (sick day rules), infection control and safety netting.
focus: Acute infectious diarrhoea in an older woman with diabetes: dehydration, AKI and sick day medication rules
stem: You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department. Linda Faulker, a 69-year-old woman, has been brought in by her husband with abdominal pain. She is on a trolley in a cubicle. A nurse has taken her first set of observations, is with you and can carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mrs Faulker and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, blood results, venous blood gas and ECG. Give an ISBAR handover that includes your interpretation, then your most likely diagnosis and differentials, your management, and your safety netting and follow-up (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Linda Faulker, a 69-year-old retired librarian. You are lying curled on your side, pale and uncomfortable, with a vomit bowl beside you. You are tired, a little embarrassed and keen to get to the toilet quickly if needed. Your husband brought you in and is in the waiting room. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining. The nurse gives the observations if asked.

Opening line: "I have this really bad tummy pain and I can't stop going to the loo."

History (give only when asked):

The pain

  • A sudden pain woke you at about 4 am, about 7 to 8 hours ago.
  • It is all over your tummy, not in one spot, and it doesn't go anywhere else.
  • It is crampy and comes in waves. Severity 6 to 7 out of 10.
  • Opening your bowels eases it for a short while, then it comes back.
  • You took two Nurofen at about 5 am, which didn't help.

Diarrhoea

  • Started soon after the pain. Loose and watery, every 1 to 2 hours, sometimes explosive.
  • No blood, no mucus, not black.
  • "It's a bit embarrassing, but I almost didn't make it to the toilet several times."

Vomiting and other symptoms

  • You have vomited 3 or 4 times today: food at first, now just clear fluid. No blood, not green.
  • You feel sick and don't want to eat. You can't keep more than sips of water down.
  • You feel "hot and cold". You haven't taken your temperature.
  • Only if asked: you are thirsty, you feel dizzy when you stand up (if the candidate tries to stand you, you are too dizzy on sitting up to stand; give the sitting values only), and you have passed only a little dark urine since this morning.
  • You haven't been able to sleep because of the pain.

Other causes (only if asked): never had anything like this before. No change in your bowels or weight loss before today. No palpitations or irregular heartbeat. No chest pain, no burning or frequency passing urine.

Source and contacts

  • "I think I picked up something from the grandkids when they were over." Charlie, your 3-year-old grandson, has been having "these wet, gross nappies".
  • The grandkids stayed over on Sunday, two days ago; you changed Charlie's nappies then, several of them.
  • No travel. Town (municipal) water. You cook your meals at home; no takeaway or unusual food.
  • Your husband is well so far.
  • No antibiotics recently and no recent hospital stays.

Past medical history: high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, reflux (GORD), carpal tunnel syndrome and osteoarthritis.

Medications:

  • Captopril 50 mg twice a day
  • Amlodipine 10 mg daily
  • Metformin XR 1000 mg daily
  • Omeprazole 20 mg daily
  • Nurofen when needed for your hands and joints
  • You took your morning tablets with a sip of water but think you may have vomited them up.

Allergies: say this only if asked directly. Penicillin: "I can't remember exactly what happens, but I think I get some kind of rash."

Family history: your mother died of a stroke at 78 and your father died of a heart attack at 83. Your son (41) and daughters (37 and 43) are well.

Social history

  • Ex-smoker: 5 cigarettes a day from age 20 to 45.
  • A glass of red wine with dinner.
  • Retired librarian. A 30-minute walk each week. Home-cooked meals.
  • You live with your husband, who is 74. You are independent with everything, although getting to the toilet in time is hard at the moment. A cleaner comes weekly.
  • Your children live nearby. "The grandkids keep me busy."

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think it's a tummy bug from the grandkids. You are embarrassed about nearly not making it to the toilet, and you worry your husband will catch it. You want something to stop the pain, vomiting and diarrhoea so you can sleep.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "It's just a bug, isn't it? Nothing serious?"

During the station:

  • If the candidate sits you up or stands you for a postural blood pressure, say you feel dizzy and lightheaded. Once you are laid flat again, the dizziness eases.
  • If the candidate gets a sitting BP of 76, lays her flat and asks the nurse to call a rapid response or the senior ED doctor and to insert a cannula for a fluid bolus, the nurse confirms she will do it now.
  • If the candidate asks the nurse for IV access, bloods, IV fluids or an antiemetic at any point, the nurse says she will do it now. Any results are given in Part 2.

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: pale, uncomfortable, lying still on her side. Alert and oriented. Weight 72 kg.
  • Observations (from the nurse): HR 124 regular, BP 96/58 lying, RR 20, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.9 °C, capillary BGL 13.4 mmol/L, pain 6/10.
  • Postural BP (only if asked): sitting up 76/48 with HR 138, and she feels dizzy.
  • Hydration: dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, cool hands, CRT 3 seconds, JVP not visible lying flat.
  • Cardiovascular and respiratory: pulse regular. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Chest clear.
  • Abdomen: not distended, no scars. Soft, with mild diffuse tenderness and no guarding or rebound. No localised tenderness in the right iliac fossa, left iliac fossa or right upper quadrant (Murphy's sign negative). No masses, no organomegaly, no pulsatile mass. Hyperactive bowel sounds. Hernial orifices clear. Renal angles not tender.
  • Rectal examination (if offered, with a chaperone): liquid brown stool, no blood or melaena, no masses.

check.x: Professionalism

Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Linda's identity, and uses contact precautions (gloves and gown, plus a surgical mask while she is vomiting) for a patient with acute diarrhoea and vomiting.
Acknowledges her pain and her embarrassment about nearly not reaching the toilet without judgement, offers an antiemetic or access to the toilet, and uses plain language throughout.
History
Characterises the abdominal pain:

kids.x: Sudden onset that woke her at about 4 am, 7 to 8 hours ago
Diffuse, crampy, no radiation, severity 6 to 7/10
Relieving factors: briefly eased by bowel motions; not helped by Nurofen

check.x: Characterises the diarrhoea:

kids.x: Onset soon after the pain, loose and watery, every 1 to 2 hours, sometimes explosive, with near incontinence
Asks specifically about blood, mucus and black stools (none)

check.x: Characterises the vomiting: 3 to 4 times today, food then clear fluid, no blood or bile, with nausea, loss of appetite, and whether she can keep fluids down.
Asks about fever and dehydration: feeling hot and cold, thirst, dizziness on standing, and reduced dark urine.

Asks about the source and risk factors: grandson Charlie's diarrhoea and the timing of the contact (nappies changed on Sunday, two days ago), travel (none), water supply (town water), food and whether anyone else is unwell, and recent antibiotics or hospital stays (none).
Screens for features of another cause: previous similar episodes, change in bowel habit or weight loss, palpitations or an irregular heartbeat, urinary symptoms and chest pain.
Takes the past medical history: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, GORD, carpal tunnel syndrome and osteoarthritis.

Takes a full medication history with doses: captopril 50 mg BD, amlodipine 10 mg daily, metformin XR 1000 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily and Nurofen as needed (taken this morning). Asks whether she has taken or vomited her morning tablets.
Asks directly about allergies and clarifies the reaction: penicillin, probably a rash.
Takes a family history: mother died of a stroke at 78, father died of an MI at 83, children well.

Takes a social history: ex-smoker (5 a day from age 20 to 45), a glass of wine with dinner, retired librarian, lives with her 74-year-old husband, independent with a weekly cleaner, and cares for her grandchildren.

Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: she thinks she caught a bug from the grandchildren, is embarrassed, worries about her husband, and wants relief so she can sleep. Responds honestly to her question (likely a bug, but needs tests and fluids because she is dry).
Examination
Asks for a full set of vital signs and a capillary BGL, and notes the tachycardia and a BP that is low for a woman on two antihypertensives.
Assesses hydration:

kids.x: Peripheral temperature and capillary refill (cool, CRT 3 seconds)

Either measures a postural BP sitting, with assistance (96/58 lying to 76/48 sitting, HR 138, dizzy), OR states that a postural BP is not needed or is unsafe because she is already tachycardic and relatively hypotensive lying down.
States that she is clinically at least moderately dehydrated

check.x: Responds to the red zone sitting SBP at once: lies her flat, escalates (rapid response or immediate senior ED review under local CERS) and asks for IV access and a crystalloid bolus.
check.d: If no postural BP was taken, award this item if the candidate asks at once for IV access, a crystalloid bolus and senior review because of the lying tachycardia and relative hypotension.

check.x: Examines the abdomen: inspection; palpation for tenderness, guarding, rebound, localised tenderness and masses (soft, mild diffuse tenderness only); percussion; bowel sounds (hyperactive); hernial orifices.
Offers a rectal examination with a chaperone (liquid brown stool, no blood).
Checks that the pulse rhythm is regular (no AF) and auscultates the heart and chest.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: lying HR 124 to 128 and SBP 96 to 94 are in the yellow zone and unchanged despite the first bolus. Recognises that the 11:55 sitting SBP of 76 was a red zone value that needed immediate escalation and a bolus at the time, and that persisting yellow zone values despite the first bolus need ongoing senior review and further fluid. May note that the BP is a large relative drop from her usual 140/80 (credited, not required).
check.d: If the 11:55 row was covered because no postural BP was taken, award on the lying yellow zone values, the lack of response to the first bolus with the need for ongoing senior review and further fluid, and the relative drop from her usual BP.

check.x: Identifies a prerenal acute kidney injury: creatinine 128 against a baseline of 70 (about 1.8 times, KDIGO stage 1) with a disproportionately raised urea of 14.8, from hypovolaemia made worse by captopril and ibuprofen.

Interprets the electrolytes and gas: hypokalaemia (3.3), mild hyponatraemia, and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.30, HCO3 18, gap about 10) from bicarbonate lost in the stool, with a normal lactate.

Interprets the other results: glucose 13.2 is hyperglycaemia of acute illness in known T2DM (ketones normal, so not DKA; glucose far below the HHS range); mildly raised WCC and CRP fit gastroenteritis; and normal lipase and LFTs argue against pancreatitis and biliary disease.
Interprets the ECG: sinus tachycardia (no AF), small U waves consistent with the hypokalaemia, QTc 450 ms, and no ischaemic ST changes.

Gives the diagnosis as acute infectious gastroenteritis, probably viral (such as norovirus), with dehydration and a prerenal AKI, justified by the sick contact, abrupt vomiting and watery diarrhoea, feeling hot and cold with a temperature of 37.9, and a soft abdomen.
Considers mesenteric ischaemia (age, vascular risk factors, sudden onset) and states that a normal lactate and soft abdomen do not exclude it.
Considers the other differentials, with a feature for or against each:

kids.x: Bacterial gastroenteritis or C. difficile (no blood, no high fever, no recent antibiotics)
Surgical causes such as appendicitis, diverticulitis or obstruction (no localising signs or peritonism)

check.x: Management

Gives a further IV crystalloid bolus (for example 500 mL Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte 148, or 0.9% sodium chloride), keeps her lying flat, and reassesses HR, BP, perfusion and urine output after each bolus; then replacement plus maintenance fluids, adding potassium once she is passing urine, with a fluid balance chart.
check.d: Moving to oral rehydration once she tolerates it is good practice but not required for the mark.

check.x: Gives an antiemetic (for example ondansetron, noting that the QTc of 450 ms is normal, but correcting potassium because hypokalaemia raises the QT risk) and paracetamol for pain, and avoids NSAIDs.
Withholds metformin, captopril, amlodipine and ibuprofen while she is dehydrated with an AKI (sick day rules), and monitors BGL 4 to 6 hourly while metformin is withheld.

Considers sepsis, because yellow zone values persist after the first bolus: takes blood cultures x2, gives a further bolus and reassesses, and discusses empirical antibiotics with a senior if she stays hypotensive (either decision earns the mark when it is justified: fluid losses explain the haemodynamics, or persistent hypotension with a fever warrants cover).

Arranges infection control: a single room with its own toilet, contact precautions, and hand washing with soap and water (alcohol rub is less effective against norovirus); sends stool PCR because she is being admitted with an AKI.

Admits her under the medical team after a registrar review, and plans to reassess the abdomen. Arranges CT angiography and a surgical review if the pain becomes constant or out of proportion, or the lactate rises.
Safety netting

Tells her in plain words, as advice for when she goes home, to come back to ED (or call 000 if she collapses) for at least 4 of: blood in the stool, pain that becomes constant, severe or in one spot, being unable to keep fluids down, dizziness or fainting, passing very little urine, high fever or confusion.

Gives a medication plan: metformin and captopril stay off until she has been eating and drinking normally for 24 to 48 hours and her UEC has been rechecked; amlodipine restarts once her BP is back towards her usual; no Nurofen, use paracetamol instead.

Arranges follow-up: GP review within a week to repeat UEC and BP and follow up the stool result. Advises hand washing and no preparing food for others or minding the grandchildren until 48 hours after symptoms stop, and checks her understanding.

part2.lead: Here are her observations, her blood results, a venous blood gas and her ECG.
part2.patient:
Ask this question once, when the candidate explains the plan:

  • "Do I need antibiotics? I'm allergic to penicillin, remember."

You are relieved if the plan is explained clearly. If the candidate uses jargon such as "AKI" or "sick day rules", ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. Postural BP at 11:55: lying 96/58 with HR 124, sitting 76/48 with HR 138, dizzy, laid flat again. CRT 3 seconds. Usual BP at the GP about 140/80.
handover.model:
• Read: at 11:50, HR 124 and lying SBP 96 are yellow zone values; RR 20, SpO2 97% on room air and alert are in the white zone; temperature 37.9 °C is low-grade; CRT 3 seconds. At 11:55 the sitting SBP of 76 is a red zone value, with HR 138 (yellow zone) and dizziness. At 12:40, after the first 500 mL, HR 128 and SBP 94 are still in the yellow zone.
  • Meaning: significant hypovolaemia. Her usual BP is about 140/80, so a lying SBP in the 90s is a large relative drop. The red zone sitting SBP needed immediate escalation (rapid response or immediate senior ED review under local CERS) and a bolus at the time, which the chart shows happened (senior review 12:00, bolus from 12:15).
  • Changes: the yellow zone values persist despite the first bolus, so she needs ongoing senior review (at least a clinical review within 30 minutes of each yellow zone set), further fluid, frequent observations and a fluid balance chart. Any further red zone value means a rapid response call.

rows.note: Triage ATS 3; vomited in the waiting room
Postural BP sitting up; dizzy, laid flat again
Senior ED MO reviewed 12:00 after red zone postural BP. Vomited and opened bowels again. Cannulated 12:05, bloods and VBG sent; first 500 mL Hartmann's bolus given 12:15 to 12:35

handover.label: Bloods
handover.model:
• Read: creatinine is 128 µmol/L against a baseline of 70, about 1.8 times baseline (KDIGO stage 1 AKI). Urea is 14.8, raised out of proportion to creatinine. eGFR 39 is not reliable during an AKI (creatinine not at steady state); use the change from baseline creatinine. Sodium 133 is mildly low, potassium 3.3 is low and bicarbonate 18 is low. Chloride and magnesium are normal. The anion gap is about 10, which is normal. Hb 148 is high-normal and may reflect haemoconcentration (no baseline). WCC 12.4 with neutrophilia and CRP 32 are mildly raised. LFTs and lipase are normal.
  • Meaning: a prerenal AKI from volume loss, made worse by captopril and ibuprofen. Potassium and bicarbonate are being lost in the stool. The mild inflammatory response fits gastroenteritis. A normal lipase and LFTs argue against pancreatitis and biliary disease.
  • Changes: IV fluids, adding potassium once she is passing urine. Withhold captopril, ibuprofen and metformin. Repeat UEC and magnesium within 24 hours.

handover.label: Venous blood gas and bedside ketones
handover.result: Venous sample at 12:05 on room air, before IV fluids. Capillary ketones at 11:55.
handover.model:
• Read: pH 7.30 is an acidaemia. Bicarbonate 18 and base excess -7 make it metabolic, with a normal anion gap (about 10) and a low-normal pCO2 from respiratory compensation. Lactate is 1.6 and normal. Glucose is 13.2 with capillary ketones of 0.3, which is normal.
  • Meaning: a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate lost in the diarrhoea. A normal lactate is reassuring against hypoperfusion, metformin-associated lactic acidosis and bowel ischaemia, but it does not exclude early mesenteric ischaemia. The raised glucose is hyperglycaemia of acute illness in known T2DM (ketones normal, so not DKA; glucose far below the HHS range).
  • Changes: rehydrate and replace potassium. Withhold metformin while she has an AKI and is dehydrated. Monitor BGL 4 to 6 hourly. Repeat lactate and reassess the abdomen if the pain changes.

handover.label: ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, 12:10. Clinical details: 69-year-old woman with vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain; K 3.3.

  • Rate: 126/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia, regular, a P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal.
  • Intervals: PR 160 ms, QRS 88 ms, QTc 450 ms.
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression. Small U waves in the precordial leads.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG available.

Conclusion: sinus tachycardia with U waves consistent with hypokalaemia; no AF or ischaemia.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 126/min, normal axis, normal PR and QRS, QTc 450 ms (normal for a woman), small U waves, no ST changes.
  • Meaning: the tachycardia fits hypovolaemia. Sinus rhythm with no AF makes an embolic cause of mesenteric ischaemia less likely but does not exclude ischaemia. The U waves fit her potassium of 3.3; U waves are more typical below 3.0 mmol/L, and at 3.3 they are subtle. No ischaemic changes argues against an atypical ACS in a woman with diabetes.
  • Changes: replace potassium, because hypokalaemia raises the QT risk with drugs such as ondansetron even though the QTc is normal, and repeat the ECG once potassium is corrected.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Linda Faulker, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Linda now, here in the emergency department.

Linda asks what she should do about her regular tablets when she goes home and whether she could pass this on to her husband or grandchildren. Please answer her, then tell me what safety netting and follow-up you would arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self (ED junior doctor); Linda Faulker, 69, in ED.
  • Situation: acute gastroenteritis with moderate dehydration and a prerenal AKI. The 11:55 sitting SBP of 76 (if that row was shown) was a red zone value that needed immediate escalation and a bolus at the time (senior ED review 12:00, bolus 12:15 to 12:35). Yellow zone values persist lying (HR 128, BP 94/54, well below her usual 140/80) despite the first bolus, so she needs ongoing senior review and further fluid.
  • Background: 8 hours of sudden diffuse crampy pain, watery diarrhoea every 1 to 2 hours without blood, vomiting 3 to 4 times, grandson with diarrhoea. Hypertension and T2DM on captopril, amlodipine and metformin; Nurofen this morning. Penicillin rash.
  • Assessment: creatinine 128 (baseline 70), urea 14.8 = prerenal AKI. K 3.3. pH 7.30, HCO3 18 = normal anion gap acidosis from stool losses. Lactate 1.6, lipase and LFTs normal. Glucose 13.2, ketones 0.3 = hyperglycaemia of acute illness in known T2DM, not DKA or HHS. WCC 12.4, CRP 32. ECG: sinus tachycardia 126, QTc 450 ms (normal), small U waves, no AF or ischaemia. Abdomen soft.
  • Recommendation: lying flat, further bolus running, medicines withheld; please review her now for admission.

Most likely: acute infectious gastroenteritis, probably viral (norovirus). Sick contact with a grandson who has diarrhoea, abrupt vomiting and watery diarrhoea, feeling hot and cold with a temperature of 37.9 °C (borderline/low-grade), crampy pain eased by bowel motions, soft abdomen. Complicated by dehydration and a prerenal AKI.

  • Bacterial gastroenteritis (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella): for: temperature 37.9 °C, cramps. Against: no blood, no high fever, no food source.
  • Mesenteric ischaemia: for: age, hypertension, diabetes, ex-smoker, sudden pain waking her. Against: pain not out of proportion, soft abdomen, sinus rhythm, normal lactate (which does not exclude it).
  • C. difficile: against: no recent antibiotics or hospital stay.
  • Appendicitis or diverticulitis: against: no localised tenderness or peritonism.

1. Lie her flat; she needs ongoing senior review (yellow zone values persist after the first bolus). Single room, contact precautions, soap and water.
  2. Further IV crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride), reassess HR, BP and urine output; then replacement plus maintenance, potassium once she is passing urine; fluid balance chart.
  3. Ondansetron (QTc 450 ms; correct potassium), paracetamol, no NSAIDs.
  4. Withhold metformin, captopril, amlodipine and ibuprofen; BGL 4 to 6 hourly.
  5. Sepsis considered: blood cultures x2; if she stays hypotensive after fluid, discuss empirical antibiotics with a senior (for infectious diarrhoea the eTG options are not penicillins; clarify the allergy if an abdominal sepsis regimen is needed). Stool PCR.
  6. Admit under medicine; CT angiography and surgical review if the pain changes or lactate rises.

• Tablets in plain words: metformin, captopril and Nurofen can harm the kidneys or build up when she is dehydrated. Metformin and captopril stay off until she has been eating and drinking normally for 24 to 48 hours and her UEC has been rechecked. Amlodipine restarts once her BP is back towards her usual. Use paracetamol, not Nurofen.
  • Spread: yes, it spreads easily. Wash hands with soap and water; do not prepare food for others or mind the grandchildren until 48 hours after symptoms stop.
  • When she goes home, come back to ED (or call 000 if she collapses) with blood in the stool, pain that becomes constant, severe or in one spot, not keeping fluids down, dizziness or fainting, passing very little urine, high fever or confusion.
  • Follow-up: GP within a week: repeat UEC and BP, restart medicines, stool result.

guide:
In Part 1, the patient answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Give the postural BP only if the candidate asks for it. Give the allergy only if asked directly. If the candidate asks for bloods or a gas in Part 1, the nurse takes them now and the results are given in Part 2. If the candidate gets the red zone sitting BP and escalates, lays her flat and asks for a cannula and a bolus, the nurse confirms she will do it now.

If the candidate did not request a postural BP in Part 1, cover or omit the 11:55 row and the postural sentence before handing over the observations. Also cover the first sentence of the 12:40 note (the senior review after the red zone postural BP), and mark the observation items on the lying values as their notes describe. In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Linda asks her question about antibiotics once, as the candidate explains the management plan.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain, diarrhoea and vomiting, asks specifically about blood in the stool, finds the sick contact and its timing and the lack of recent antibiotics, and takes a full medication and allergy history. They assess hydration, either taking a postural BP with assistance or stating that it is not needed because she is already tachycardic and relatively hypotensive lying down. If they find the red zone sitting BP, they act on it at once. They examine the abdomen properly and check the pulse rhythm. In Part 2 they recognise the persisting yellow zone lying observations, the red zone sitting SBP that needed immediate escalation at the time, the prerenal AKI, the normal anion gap acidosis, the hyperglycaemia of acute illness in known diabetes and the hypokalaemic ECG. They give gastroenteritis as the diagnosis while still respecting mesenteric ischaemia in a 69-year-old with vascular risk factors. They resuscitate with IV fluids, withhold metformin, captopril, amlodipine and NSAIDs, avoid unnecessary antibiotics, arrange infection control, and give specific red flags and a plan for restarting her medicines.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history, does not ask about blood or her medicines, misses the significance of the lying tachycardia and relative hypotension (and of the red zone sitting BP if obtained), and calls the creatinine "a bit high" without comparing it to baseline. They may prescribe antibiotics routinely, continue all her regular tablets, or discharge her with vague advice. Accept any reasonable isotonic crystalloid and antiemetic. Credit "SADMANS" or "sick day rules" if the candidate names the right drugs.
explain:
Diagnosis

Acute infectious gastroenteritis means diarrhoea of rapid onset, lasting less than 14 days, with or without nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or fever. Linda had an abrupt onset of crampy diffuse pain, watery diarrhoea without blood, vomiting and a borderline temperature of 37.9 °C, two days after changing the nappies of a grandson with diarrhoea. This is typical of a viral cause, most often norovirus in adults (rotavirus mainly affects young children). Other causes in Australia are Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, C. difficile and toxin-mediated S. aureus. Most cases settle on their own. In an older woman with diabetes on an ACE inhibitor, metformin and NSAIDs, the danger is the complications: dehydration, acute kidney injury and drug toxicity.

What the history must cover

  • Severity: how often she vomits and passes stool, whether she can keep fluids down, dizziness, urine output, fever.
  • Red flags for invasive or other disease: blood or mucus in the stool, high fever, severe or localised pain.
  • Source and contacts: sick contacts and when the contact happened, travel, water, food, and others affected (outbreaks).
  • Recent antibiotics or hospital stays (C. difficile).
  • Medicines that become dangerous when she is dehydrated.

Assessing hydration

Lying flat she is already tachycardic (HR 124) with an SBP of 96, well below her usual 140/80, with cool peripheries, a CRT of 3 seconds and little urine. That is enough to diagnose significant hypovolaemia. A postural BP adds little and can make her faint, so it is reasonable either to take one carefully, with assistance, or to say it is not needed. If it is done and the sitting SBP falls into the red zone, the response is immediate: lie her flat, escalate and give a fluid bolus then, not after the results come back.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: tachycardia and a lying systolic BP in the 90s are yellow zone values on the NSW adult chart and need a clinical review. Her sitting SBP of 76, a symptomatic 20/10 mmHg postural fall, is a red zone value: lie her flat, escalate at once (rapid response or immediate senior review under local CERS) and give a fluid bolus. Yellow zone values that persist after the first bolus need ongoing senior review and further fluid. For a woman who normally runs about 140/80 on two antihypertensives, this is a large relative drop and confirms significant volume depletion.
  • Kidneys: creatinine has risen to about 1.8 times baseline with a disproportionately raised urea. This is a prerenal AKI (KDIGO stage 1), made worse by an ACE inhibitor (which blocks efferent arteriolar constriction) and an NSAID (which blocks afferent prostaglandin dilation).
  • Electrolytes and gas: diarrhoea loses potassium and bicarbonate, giving hypokalaemia and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (chloride is relatively high for a sodium of 133, although within the reference range). Large volumes of 0.9% sodium chloride can worsen a hyperchloraemic acidosis, so a balanced crystalloid is preferred.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia with small U waves from the hypokalaemia, no AF and no ischaemic changes. U waves are more typical below 3.0 mmol/L; at 3.3 they are subtle. The QTc of 450 ms is normal for a woman, but hypokalaemia raises the QT risk with drugs such as ondansetron, so correct the potassium and repeat the ECG.
  • Lactate: a normal lactate is reassuring, but it does not exclude early mesenteric ischaemia.
  • Glucose: hyperglycaemia of acute illness in known T2DM (ketones normal, so not DKA; glucose far below the HHS range).
  • Full blood count: Hb 148 is high-normal and may reflect haemoconcentration (no baseline). The mildly raised WCC and CRP fit gastroenteritis.

Differentials that matter

  • Mesenteric ischaemia is the diagnosis not to miss in an older person with vascular risk factors and sudden pain. Look for pain out of proportion to the examination, AF and a rising lactate, and arrange CT mesenteric angiography if it is suspected.
  • Bacterial enteritis is more likely with bloody diarrhoea, high fever or a food source.
  • C. difficile follows antibiotic exposure or a hospital stay; PPIs are also a risk factor.
  • Appendicitis, diverticulitis and early obstruction usually give localised tenderness, peritonism or distension.

Management (eTG Acute infectious diarrhoea)

  • Rehydration is the mainstay. Oral rehydration solution is preferred when it is tolerated. IV isotonic crystalloid is used for significant dehydration or ongoing vomiting, with frequent reassessment and replacement of potassium once urine output is confirmed. An antiemetic can help oral intake.
  • Antimotility agents may be used for watery diarrhoea in adults but are avoided with bloody diarrhoea, high fever or suspected C. difficile.
  • Antibiotics are not needed for most cases. Empirical treatment is reserved for severe illness (for example sepsis or dysentery) or immunocompromise. For Linda: sepsis considered (suspected infection with red and yellow zone observations): blood cultures taken, lactate normal, her losses may explain the haemodynamics, but she has not fully responded to the first bolus, so she gets a further bolus and a senior review, and empirical antibiotics are started if she stays hypotensive after fluid or the fever or lactate rises. Under the NSW SEPSIS KILLS pathway her red zone value with suspected infection triggers a sepsis screen (lactate, blood cultures x2); withholding antibiotics because her losses explain the haemodynamics is a senior decision and is documented. If antibiotics are needed for severe infectious diarrhoea, the eTG options (azithromycin or ciprofloxacin) are not penicillins, so her penicillin rash does not limit them; azithromycin, like ondansetron, prolongs the QT, so correct her potassium first. If sepsis from an abdominal source such as ischaemic bowel were being treated, the usual regimens include a penicillin and her allergy then matters: clarify the reaction and follow the eTG alternative.
  • Stool testing is not routine. Test when the illness is severe (blood, high fever, tachycardia, leucocytosis, severe pain, hypovolaemia), the patient is immunocompromised, there is an outbreak, or there has been recent antibiotic exposure. Linda's hypovolaemia, AKI and admission justify a stool PCR.

Sick day rules

Medicines that harm the kidneys or accumulate when a patient is dehydrated are withheld until the patient is eating and drinking normally (commonly 24 to 48 hours) and renal function has been checked. They are often remembered as SADMANS: sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, metformin, angiotensin receptor blockers, NSAIDs and SGLT2 inhibitors. Amlodipine is held while she is hypotensive and restarted once her BP is back towards her usual. Her BGL is monitored while metformin is withheld, because illness raises glucose.

Infection control and public health

Norovirus spreads easily. In hospital she needs a single room with her own toilet and contact precautions. Hands should be washed with soap and water, because alcohol rub is less reliable against norovirus. At home, she should not prepare food for others or care for the grandchildren until 48 hours after her symptoms stop, and the bathroom should be cleaned with a chlorine-based product. Outbreaks of 2 or more linked cases in a facility such as an aged care home or childcare centre are notified to the public health unit.

Safety netting

Linda should return for blood in the stool, worsening or localised pain, being unable to keep fluids down, dizziness or fainting, very little urine, high fever or confusion. She should call 000 if she collapses. A GP review within a week rechecks her kidney function and BP before her medicines are restarted.
points: Acute infectious diarrhoea is diarrhoea of rapid onset lasting under 14 days. It is usually viral (norovirus in adults) and self-limiting, and rehydration is the mainstay of treatment.

Ask specifically about blood in the stool, high fever, severe or localised pain, recent antibiotics and sick contacts: these change the diagnosis, the need for stool tests and the need for antibiotics.

Tachycardia and relative hypotension while lying flat already show significant hypovolaemia; a postural BP is optional. A red zone value, including a postural one, needs escalation and a fluid bolus at the time, not after the results return.
In an older patient with vascular risk factors and sudden abdominal pain, keep mesenteric ischaemia in mind. A soft abdomen and a normal lactate do not fully exclude it.

Dehydration with an ACE inhibitor and an NSAID causes a prerenal AKI. Withhold metformin, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors and sulfonylureas (SADMANS) until the patient is eating and drinking normally and renal function is checked.

Diarrhoea causes hypokalaemia and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis; replace potassium with the fluids. Antibiotics and stool testing are not routine, and suspected norovirus needs contact precautions and soap-and-water hand washing.

ddx.dx: Acute infectious gastroenteritis, probably viral (norovirus), with dehydration and prerenal acute kidney injury
ddx.for: Abrupt vomiting and watery diarrhoea two days after changing her grandson's diarrhoeal nappies, temperature 37.9 °C, crampy pain eased by bowel motions and a soft abdomen with hyperactive bowel sounds.
ddx.against: Pain severe enough to wake her in a 69-year-old with vascular risk factors means other causes must still be considered.

ddx.for: Temperature 37.9 °C, crampy pain, WCC 12.4 with neutrophilia and CRP 32.
ddx.against: No blood or mucus in the stool, no high fever, no food source or travel, and a clear sick contact with a viral pattern.

ddx.for: Age 69 with hypertension, diabetes, a smoking history and sudden pain that woke her.
ddx.against: Pain not out of proportion, soft abdomen, sinus rhythm with no AF and lactate 1.6, although a normal lactate does not exclude it.

ddx.for: Frequent watery diarrhoea while taking daily omeprazole.
ddx.against: No recent antibiotics or hospital stay, and a sick contact with similar symptoms.

ddx.for: Abdominal pain with a low-grade fever, WCC 12.4 and CRP 32 in an older woman.
ddx.against: Diffuse pain with no localised tenderness in either iliac fossa and no guarding or rebound.
